beats.narration_text: Bonjour. This is Liam, in for Bear. In C S Y E seven two seven zero, the A. I. works under a set of rules called Walker. The shortcut is to picture Walker as software that stops the A. I. from doing wrong. This film shows what it really is: a written set of rules and a habit, and what that can and cannot do.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. Walker is a framework: written instructions and a few tools for building games with an A. I. agent. A game design document is the written description of what the game is. A play-test is a person playing the game to see how it feels. A gate is a point where work stops until a person approves. And a convention is a rule that is followed because it was asked, not because anything enforces it.

terms.meaning: written instructions and tools for building games with an AI agent
the written description of what the game is
a person playing the game to see how it feels
a point where work stops until a person approves
a rule followed because it was asked, not enforced

beats.act: II · The Loop and Who Decides
beats.narration_text: Walker's working loop has six steps. Game brief. Build. Play-test. Inspect. Revise. Export.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'The Loop and Who Decides' (size 40) over a ring of six outlined nodes: Game brief (upper left), Build (top), Play-test (upper right), Inspect (lower right), Revise (bottom), Export (lower left), each labelled beside its node. The six nodes appear one by one on 'six steps'. In the middle first sits the REAL GAME-BRIEF.md (file name in Menlo, its promise line 'I can see why that failed, and I want one more try.', 'line 11'); a terracotta dot lands on Game brief, then travels the ring node by node on each spoken name, filling each node and drawing the ring in ink behind it. On 'Build' the brief gives way to the REAL recorded run of the walker-claude Godot game (Clawd running and jumping, frames of the capture stepped in time), captioned 'recorded run, scripted input'; at 'Export' the ring closes back to the brief.

show.event: six nodes appear one by one
dot lands on Game brief (midpoint frame: brief card in the centre)
Build: card replaced by the real recorded game, caption

shot.motion_claim: The dot walks the loop on the spoken names and the ring closes; the game the loop produces plays in the middle.

lecture.runner_up: Remotion LibraryIconRow of six marks in a row; and a ring with a real capture thumbnail at every node
lecture.why: A loop is a circle you travel: only a moving dot closing the ring shows 'loop' (a row of marks reads as a list). One thumbnail per step would map a scripted recording onto steps it did not perform (the recording is not a play-test), so the real game plays once in the middle as 'what the loop produces', labelled recorded run, scripted input.

beats.act: II · The Loop and Who Decides
beats.narration_text: Each step produces something, and stops somewhere. Build produces a runnable project, not a claim that it is finished. Export produces a package and evidence. Publishing is a separate step.

On 'stops somewhere' an ink stop bar closes every row at the right edge. On 'Build produces' every other row steps back to grey and the Build row stays ink with a terracotta dot ('Runnable project … not a completion claim'); on 'Export produces' the focus moves to the Export row ('Versioned package and evidence;'); on 'Publishing' an arrow runs down from that row and stops at a heavy wall, with the rest of the cell, 'publication remains separate', beneath it.

beats.act: III · What the AI Must Not Do
beats.narration_text: Now the part you came for: what the A. I. must not do. Start with scope. It must not switch engines silently. It must not cut requirements, stretch the schedule, spend money or publish, just to keep the loop running.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'What the AI Must Not Do' (size 40). Left: two rule slips (outlined cards) quoting zelda-gdd.md:13 ('Do not silently use Unity, Bevy, Babylon.js, or a hosted game generator.') and zelda-gdd.md:40 ('Do not cut requirements, extend schedules, spend, publish … just to keep a loop running.'), each with its file:line in Menlo and a 'doc' tag. Right: 'scope' header; a tall outlined track labelled 'loop' with the agent (a terracotta dot) on it; five exits to the right, each ending in an ink barrier and a label (switch engine, cut requirements, extend schedule, spend money, publish); a legend of the three where-it-lives tags (installed / doc / game file).

beats.act: III · What the AI Must Not Do
beats.narration_text: Drafting a task is not permission to run it. A direct request for a complete draft allows the draft, with its assumptions named. It does not allow inventing approvals.

beats.act: III · What the AI Must Not Do
beats.narration_text: Then, proof. Judge progress from the running game, never from a clean build. A successful build is not evidence of a successful human play-test. The game's own file adds: never invent human play-tests or test passes. And if a test fails, never weaken the test to make it pass.

shot.visual_intent: Left: a window playing the REAL run of the Walker Jumpman game with Clawd (frames of EVID/godot-captures/walker-claude/walker-claude-jumpman-gameplay.mp4, scripted input recorded 2026-10-09, looped), captioned 'recorded run, looping' and 'scripted input, 2026-10-09'. While the voice says 'build is not a play-test' the run steps aside and the idea is drawn large (build with a check, does-not-equal, an empty dashed 'human play-test'); the run returns after the midpoint captioned 'scripted input: not a play-test'. Right: one rule slip at a time: runtime.md:10 [installed], README.md:28 [doc], AGENTS.md:13 [game file], zelda-gdd.md:52 [doc], each verbatim with a cut marked; the 'game file' pill of the AGENTS.md:13 slip lands on the spoken "The game's own file adds". Bottom: four small cards (running game / not a play-test / invented passes / weakened test) with drawn glyphs, lit one by one.

beats.act: III · What the AI Must Not Do
beats.narration_text: Then, money and safety. The asset tools call paid services, and every call costs real money, so the agent confirms before the first. Never commit credentials. Writing files on your own computer is not publishing to GitHub. Uploading is a separate action.

Credentials: a key drawn toward a 'commit' box and stopped at a barrier; slip README.md:71 [doc]. Publishing: a 'computer' box with a page written inside it, an arrow with a barrier toward a 'GitHub' box labelled 'separate action'; slip README.md:63 [doc].

beats.act: IV · How the AI Writes Code
beats.narration_text: How the agent writes the code is covered too, in two layers. Layer one is installed in every game: a Godot guide. It says build, then import, then run headless. Verify against the installed Godot instead of guessing its interface. And judge from the running game.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'How the AI Writes Code' (serif 40) top-left. On 'two layers' two stacked slabs numbered 1 and 2 (top right); on 'Layer one is installed in every game' a terracotta spark lands on slab 1, the chip 'Layer one: installed in every game' and an outline frame headed by a page mark and `godot.md` appear. Inside, the REAL build gate from godot.md:10 as three numbered Menlo lines (`dotnet build` / `godot --headless --import` + 'after asset changes' / `godot --headless --quit`) joined by arrows, appearing as each is spoken. Right column: the real godot.md:49 fragment 'Verify against the installed Godot …' with a magnifier mark, then the real CLAUDE.md:10 fragment 'Judge progress from the running game …' with a terracotta play mark; each quote carries its file:line.
shot.motion_claim: The three commands arrive in the order spoken, arrows between them; then the verify rule, then the running-game rule.

lecture.runner_up: CCPlainShell terminal skin showing the three commands as if run (Remotion)
lecture.why: the commands are a rule in a file, not a run: showing godot.md as text with its file:line is the thing itself; a terminal skin would imply they were executed. The ordered arrows are the claim 'build, then import, then run headless'.

beats.act: IV · How the AI Writes Code
beats.narration_text: Layer two is a set of conventions for G D script. Type every variable. Children talk to parents with signals, never by reaching up the tree. Build small, single-purpose scenes. The Clawd game also keeps each feature's files together.

shot.visual_intent: Header 'Layer two: conventions for GDScript' (serif 40) with slab 2 and a spark, and the real file name godot-scripting-conventions-research-prompt.md (Menlo). Four rows, each a small drawn icon + the prompt's own words with its line tag: (1) variable box with a type tag + `var hp: int = 100` (L137); (2) child box signalling up to a parent box (a terracotta pulse travels up), then a grey reach-around path struck with an X + `Never call a method on get_parent()` (L158); (3) a box that fills with three small boxes + 'composing small, single-purpose scenes/components' (L167); (4) a folder with three file marks + the REAL folder of the Clawd game, `features/player/` holding player.gd, tuning.gd, clawd_art.gd (labelled 'Kept together in the Clawd game', matching the re-voiced last sentence).
shot.motion_claim: Four icons arrive one per spoken convention; the signal pulse travels up the arrow, the reach-up route gets crossed out, three small scenes fill one box, three files drop into one folder.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage with the voice carrying the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.runner_up: CCPlainShell / Remotion code card with four numbered code snippets
lecture.why: each convention has one tiny mechanism the voice can point at (a pulse that goes UP a signal, a crossed-out reach-around, parts filling a scene, files dropping into one folder); a code card would show four lines of text and no mechanism. All lines are the real prompt's own, with line tags. Cues from faster-whisper word times (evidence/act4/word_times.json).

beats.narration_text: I ran Walker's publisher for real. One command. Six lines of output. It installed fifty-four files: a twelve-line instruction file, a Godot guide, a settings file that ignores generated files, and two skills. No game.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Walker in Action' (serif 40) top-left. A grey terminal outline labelled 'recorded run, 2026-10-09' types the REAL command (wrapped, scratch path trimmed with an ellipsis) and prints the six real output lines of publish.log. The terminal fades; hero '54 files / 127,260 bytes' appears and six file rows land one per spoken noun: CLAUDE.md 12 lines, godot.md 66 lines, .gitignore 9 lines, asset-gen/ 8 files, gdd/ 43 files, and a dashed empty row 'game 0 files'.
shot.motion_claim: One command types and the real output prints; then the 54 files land as the voice names them, and the last row stays empty: no game.

qc.sparse_reason: two real facts per frame (a terminal; a tally of six rows); the log is the evidence, not decoration

lecture.runner_up: Remotion CCPlainShell with the real command and the 6 output lines (rendered and looked at at 50%): faithful dark terminal skin, the whole command on one line, but it sits unchanged for the beat and cannot hold the 54-file tally, the counts or the empty 'game' row
lecture.why: the terminal skin is the real run, but the claim is the tally: Manim carries both the real log text and the rows that land on each spoken noun, ending on the empty 'game' row

beats.narration_text: Here is the twelve-line instruction file. It tells the agent to build from the design document, not from memory of the chat. To judge progress from the running game. And to finish with a short video of the game, and watch it back before calling the work done.

shot.visual_intent: The real 12-line CLAUDE.md as a ruled page (twelve slots, bar lengths from the real character counts; blank lines are gaps) named 'CLAUDE.md' '12 lines'. As each instruction is spoken a terracotta dot marks its line and the real words lift out beside the page in Menlo with 'line N of 12': line 5 (design/GDD.md, not memory of the chat), line 10 (judge progress from the running game), line 12 twice (the 15-20s video, with its condition; watch it back).

show.event: line 12: the video, with its condition

shot.motion_claim: The page's lines light up in turn exactly as the voice reads them, and the real sentence lifts out.

qc.sparse_reason: one page and one quoted line at a time: the claim is one line at a time

lecture.runner_up: Remotion CCPlainShell with the file as text: 12 lines hold ~13 lines of ~66 columns but line 12 is 553 characters, so most of the file would be wrapped or cut, and a line cannot be highlighted
lecture.why: the file's real shape (three long lines among short ones) is itself information, and Manim can light one line and lift its real words at the spoken word

beats.narration_text: Now the rules at work, on one real change: turning the player into Clawd. One change, not the whole game. Three predicted failures, named in the brief. Physics left alone.

shot.visual_intent: REAL Godot output in a grey window (stepped real frames at real time, scripted input, labelled 'recorded run, scripted input'). 'the player': the starter game's original player (real capture of the same level) runs and jumps; just after the clip midpoint it swaps to the REAL Clawd run of the same level and the label becomes 'the player: Clawd'. 'scope: drawing only' (terracotta dot) lands on 'One change'; then three outlined cards 'Predicted failures': 1 Wide arms overhang, 2 Two jump arcs, 3 Gallery read as gameplay; then a check 'physics untouched'.

show.event: starter player runs and jumps (real time)
swap to the real Clawd run; 'the player: Clawd'

shot.motion_claim: The same level, the same run: the starter's player is replaced by Clawd while the rules land beside it: scope first, then each prediction, then the check on physics.

qc.sparse_reason: a real game window (5.5 wide, never enlarged past the capture's pixel density) and three short cards

lecture.runner_up: ShowTellCard (document kind) with the three predictions as a page: passes the card test only if the page matters more than the game; here the game output is the evidence and must stay on screen. Also auditioned: Clawd from frame 0 (failed GATE T's terracotta-accent test at the 50% sample: the flat #dd775b body is read as a text run), hence the starter 'before' first
lecture.why: real engine output is the picture wherever the narration is about the game; the before/after (starter player, then Clawd) is the change itself, and the rules are short labels beside it

beats.narration_text: The first prediction came true. The broad arms stick out past the left edge, and the character passes in front of world labels. The record leaves it open, for a person to judge in play.

shot.visual_intent: Two real Godot windows. Left: five real frames (scripted run of the same Godot project, Left held; cropped to the bottom-left strip so the level's dark blocks stay out) of Clawd reaching the left wall and being cut off by the edge, 'past the left edge'. Right (starts just after the midpoint): four real clip frames of Clawd passing over the label 'Read the landing. Then jump.', 'over world labels'. A check 'predicted: wide arms', then a dashed open ring 'open: a person judges' with FRICTIONAL.md:59-63.

show.event: left: run to the wall, cut by the edge

shot.motion_claim: Both observed problems are shown happening in the real game; the ring that stays open is the record leaving it to a human.

qc.sparse_reason: two real windows (the right one lands just after the 50% sample so a whole Clawd body is not on screen then) and one status row

lecture.runner_up: ShowTellCard (document) with the FRICTIONAL.md lines as text: the quote is in the closing source tag, but the claim is visible behaviour and only the frames show it. Also auditioned: full 1080 px crops of both windows (failed GATE T per-blob contrast at 50%: the level's dark step block on its green top reads as a text blob), hence the narrower crop
lecture.why: the voice states two visible things; each is shown in the real game, so the picture is evidence, not a description

beats.narration_text: The proof rules caught things too. A recording with a pass receipt had only three hundred and forty-three of five hundred and forty frames. Rejected, and kept. Another ended with exit code zero and no receipt. Rejected, and kept. The rule was: preserve failed receipts.

shot.visual_intent: Two real receipts as outlined pages. 'gallery-two': the real lines "status": "PASS", "frames": 343, a bar filling to 343 against 540 expected (terracotta dot at the fill end), then a cross 'rejected' and a page 'kept'. 'inspector-v2': the real line "exit_code": 0, a dashed empty page 'no receipt', cross 'rejected', page 'kept'. Last: 'Preserve failed receipts.' with AGENTS.md:15.
shot.motion_claim: The PASS receipt fills only 343 of 540 and is rejected; the exit-zero take has nothing behind it and is rejected; both stay on the shelf.

qc.sparse_reason: two receipts and one rule, one idea each

lecture.runner_up: Remotion CCPlainShell showing the two JSON files: the PASS lines would show, but not the shortfall (343 of 540) that makes the PASS a lie
lecture.why: the point is the gap between a PASS word and a frame count, which a bar shows and a text block cannot

beats.narration_text: And what did a human find? The record holds no human finding. The play-test is marked pending. The four design gates are unsigned. The rule says never invent them, and it was followed.

shot.visual_intent: A dashed empty page 'human finding' that stays empty ('none on record', dashed open ring). Beside it the real status files: CLAWD-STATUS.json "human_playtest": "pending" types in; DESIGN-STATUS.json lists vision, systems, world, scope each with "signed_by": null. Last: 'Never invent human playtests, ... approvals or test passes.' AGENTS.md:13 and a check.
shot.motion_claim: The question's page stays empty while the real files fill with pending and null; the rule's check lands last.

qc.sparse_reason: an empty page, two real excerpts and a rule; the emptiness is the point

lecture.runner_up: ShowTellCard (document) with the two files: shows the values but not the empty page that answers 'what did a human find?'
lecture.why: the answer to the question is an absence; an empty page beside the real null/pending lines shows it

beats.narration_text: So what is Walker not? It is not an enforcer. Gates are recorded in a status file the agent could edit. Walker's own document says gate validation is a convention the skill follows, not code that enforces it.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'What Walker Is Not' (serif 40) top-left. The REAL design-status file of the Clawd game drawn as itself: 'design/DESIGN-STATUS.json' in Menlo and its four gate rows (vision, systems, world, scope), each with the file's exact text '"signed_by": null'. An open padlock drawn beside it ('no lock', a drawing of the idea). A blinking edit caret after the first null, the file's real mode '-rw-r--r--' ('plain file, owner can write'), Walker's own sentence (13 words, 'zelda-gdd-workflow.md, line 66, local copy'), and the file's own note 'Gates are signed by humans only.'

show.event: panel + file name + four gate rows
a terracotta dot beside each gate row
edit caret after the first null, blinking
real mode -rw-r--r-- and 'plain file, owner can write'

shot.motion_claim: The padlock is drawn closed, then its shackle lifts open on 'not an enforcer'; a caret blinks in the gate file on 'the agent could edit'; the quote lands on 'Walker's own document says'; the open lock pulses on 'not code that enforces it'.

qc.sparse_reason: one file panel and a short quote on cream; every label that matters is settled by the 50% frame; the file text is real, not padding

lecture.runner_up: Remotion CCPlainShell showing the file as a terminal `cat`; Manim wins because the claim is that the gate file is editable, so the file is drawn as an object with a caret in it (a cat would be a still listing)
lecture.why: The real file and its real mode are the evidence; a drawn lock and a blinking caret carry 'not an enforcer' and 'could edit' as motion on the spoken words

beats.narration_text: It is not finished. The command-line adapter is still a specification. Walker ships no test framework. And on the day this was recorded, the public version on GitHub installed only the asset tool, an eleven-line instruction file, a Godot guide and an ignore file. The larger kit was not yet published.

shot.visual_intent: Part 1: a 'Not finished' ledger of two dashed cells (drawn, not built): the real run '$ walker gdd' with its real output 'zsh:1: command not found: walker' (recorded run, this Mac, 9 October 2026; 'still a specification') and 'test framework' ('none ships with Walker', repo searched). Part 2: the ledger clears; the REAL public GitHub page of the repo, cropped to its six folder names (asset-gen, docs, engines, legacy, prompts, scripts), captioned 'public page, captured 9 Oct 2026'. Then two bars of the real publisher file counts: '11 files, public, on GitHub' (asset tool 8 + CLAUDE.md, godot.md, .gitignore) and '54 files, local copy' (the same 11 plus a dashed segment 'the /gdd skill, 43 files', 'not on the page above').

show.event: real output: zsh:1: command not found: walker
CLAUDE.md segment (3 files) and its label

shot.motion_claim: Each dashed 'not built' cell is drawn on its spoken phrase; the real page arrives on 'the public version on GitHub'; the public bar grows on 'asset tool' and 'eleven-line instruction file', its godot.md / .gitignore label lands on 'Godot guide' and 'ignore file', then '11 files'; the local bar and its dashed 43-file segment are drawn on 'the larger kit was not yet published'.

qc.sparse_reason: the 50% frame holds the real public page and its caption (the counts arrive on their spoken words after it); the picture is real evidence, not padding

lecture.runner_up: Remotion BrowserCapture with camera moves on the full github-walker.png plus a CCPlainShell for the command; Manim wins because the beat needs two real artifacts, a counted comparison and a ledger on one stage, and BrowserCapture would hold one full page while the voice talks about two files
lecture.why: Real run, real page and real counts shown as themselves; the two bars make 11 against 54 and the missing 43 visible, which a table of numbers would not

beats.narration_text: So why use it? Because a rule written down is a rule you can check the agent against. The value is the habit. Predict. Change one thing. Run the real game. Keep the failed receipts. And leave the judgment to the human.

shot.visual_intent: Part 1: a real rule from the installed instructions ('Judge progress from the running game, never from a clean build', CLAUDE.md, line 10, installed by Walker's publisher) with an arrow to a real frame of the running Clawd game ('the running game', recorded run, scripted input, 9 October 2026). Part 2: 'The habit' as five verbs down the left (Predict. Change one thing. Run the real game. Keep the failed receipts. Leave the judgment to the human.), each with the real exhibit it came from in Act V: three numbered cells 'in the change brief'; 'drawing only' and 'physics left alone'; 'LEVEL COMPLETE deaths=0 time=5.63', the game's own log; '343 of 540 frames' 'said PASS' and 'exit 0, no receipt'; '"human_playtest": "pending"'. A loop arrow runs from the last row back to the first.

shot.motion_claim: The arrow from the rule to the running game draws on 'check the agent against'; the five verbs stand as the habit, then each row's real exhibit lands on its spoken verb; the loop arrow closes on 'to the human'.

qc.sparse_reason: text and exhibit rows on cream; the 50% frame holds the heading, the five verbs and the first exhibit

lecture.runner_up: Remotion LibraryIconRow with five icons for the verbs; rejected because the claim is that each verb is a real exhibit from the record, and icons would stand for exhibits instead of showing them
lecture.why: Five verbs, each tied to the real thing it was in Act V, so the recap is evidence and not a slogan; the rule-to-game check opens the beat on the sentence about checking

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Walker is written rules and a habit, not software. The loop: brief, build, play-test, inspect, revise, export. The human decides what the game is and whether it feels right. No silent scope, no invented approvals, no weakened tests. The installed guide and the example games disagree on language. A rule you can check is a rule you can hold the agent to.

show.event: six recap lines land in narration order

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write me a manifest for building a small game with you, in at most twelve lines. It must say what you must not do without my approval, what counts as proof that something works, and which decisions only I can make. Then tell me which of those rules you could break without anything stopping you. Then check two things yourself. Does each rule name something you can look at in the running game? And do you know which rules are only conventions?
